segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants walked from the sky to the trees and, last of all, to me. Today the peace has to work in a smaller space: one room, three people, a deadline.

Group projects tend to reach a moment: one deadline, a shared doc, and each person quietly sure the others are the problem. Priya's assembly team hit it last night. One senior wants to cut half the readings to save time, Sam is furious, and Priya is in the middle. Is there a chant for that? There's a hymn for it, near the very end of the Rig Veda. It isn't one of the Upanishads' peace chants, but some gatherings close with it, and it speaks straight to a room like this one.
screen: `PRIYA, IN THE MIDDLE.` → `A HYMN FOR A ROOM LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: It opens: sam gacchadhvam, sam vadadhvam, sam vo manamsi janatam. Word by word. Sam: together. Gacchadhvam: go, said to a group, all of you. The ending -dhvam is how Sanskrit gives a direction to many people at once. Not the dual this time, not just two. Everyone. Vadadhvam: speak, all of you. Vo: your. Manamsi: minds. Janatam: may they know, may they understand. So: go together, speak together, may your minds come to know as one. A few verses on, the hymn asks that people's aims be shared and their hearts alike, so that they may be well together. Now look closely at what it doesn't ask. It doesn't ask anyone to become the same person, or to stop talking. Both verbs are about moving and speaking. The people stay many; the -dhvam ending keeps them plural the whole way through. What the hymn wants is agreement on the way forward: a shared aim, carried by different voices. That's a sentence a parent could say at dinner, too: we don't have to be the same to go the same way.
screen: `SAM: TOGETHER.` · `-DHVAM: ALL OF YOU, GO, SPEAK.` · `MINDS THAT COME TO KNOW AS ONE.` · `STILL MANY VOICES.` · then, large: `NOT THE SAME. THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: Pick one conversation in your life that's stuck. Name, silently, what you most want from it, then the thing most likely to get in the way, then one sentence you could say first that moves toward the shared aim. Sit with that sentence for the rest of the time.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: sam gacchadhvam, go together, from a Rig Veda hymn said to many people at once.
screen: `THE GAYATRI AND THE PEACE CHANTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road: the Gayatri and the peace chants understood word by word, many voices, one way forward. Goodnight, or good morning.

notes: Peace chants, day 4 of 4. RV 10.191 is not a shanti patha of the Upanishads; the script says so plainly and calls it 'a hymn near the very end of the Rig Veda' (it is 10.191, the closing hymn of the collection). The title's 'peace chants' is read broadly here; a Keeper may prefer a shanti patha instead.

RV 10.191.2 from memory: saṃ gacchadhvaṃ saṃ vadadhvaṃ saṃ vo manāṃsi jānatām. 10.191.4: samānī va ākūtiḥ samānā hṛdayāni vaḥ, samānam astu vo mano yathā vaḥ susahāsati (paraphrased). Confirm. 'Janatam: may they know' glossed simply; with sam it means 'agree, know together'.
'Some gatherings close with it' (howItsDone: 'some Hindu gatherings and organizations') is general; confirm.
